notes: Wisdom, skill, or insight. In Greek culture it meant philosophy and clever speech, and in Jewish writings it often meant practical, God-given insight for living well. In this letter Paul sets "the wisdom of this age" against God's wisdom, which looks like foolishness because it is centered on a crucified Messiah (1:18-2:16).

elsewhere.note: Wisdom speaks about her place in creation.
In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom.
The wisdom from above is pure and peaceable.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Foolishness. The English word "moron" comes from the same root. Paul says the message of the cross looks like foolishness to the world, and then says God's "foolishness" is wiser than human wisdom (1:18-25).

range.note: What the cross looks like to the world.

elsewhere.note: The natural person finds God's things foolishness.
The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To boast or glory in something. Paul uses it often in this letter, usually against boasting in people, and says the only fitting boast is "in the Lord," echoing Jeremiah 9:24 (1:29-31).

range.note: Speak proudly of oneself or others.

elsewhere.note: We boast in sufferings.
May I never boast except in the cross.
Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A tear or split, as in cloth or a crowd. In this letter it names divisions in the church (1:10; 11:18; 12:25). It does not necessarily mean separate churches, but a breakdown of unity inside one.

elsewhere.note: A division arose among the crowd because of him.
A division among them over Jesus.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: What a herald announces. It stands for the content of the message that is preached, not the style of delivery. Paul says God was pleased to save people through the "foolishness of the preached message" (1:21).

elsewhere.note: My gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ.
Through me the proclamation might be fully made.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Paul makes the cross the center of his message to Corinth (1:17-18, 1:23, 2:2).

range.note: The wooden frame used for crucifixion.
A picture of giving up one's life.

elsewhere.note: They compelled Simon to carry his cross.
Boast only in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "The message of the cross is the power of God" (1:18, 1:24; 2:4-5).

elsewhere.note: The gospel is the power of God for salvation.
You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The Corinthians are "called to be saints" (1:2), and Christ is God's power and wisdom "to those who are called" (1:24).

elsewhere.note: Paul, called to be an apostle.
Called to be saints.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "To Jews a stumbling block" (1:23).

range.note: The part of a trap that snaps shut.
Something that makes a person fall.

elsewhere.note: I lay in Zion a stumbling stone.
Then the offense of the cross has been removed.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Belonging to the Spirit, or shaped by the Spirit. In this letter it describes people, gifts, and things. Paul uses it against those who treated being "spiritual" as a proud status. For him it means to be led by God's Spirit (2:13-15; 12:1; 14:1; 15:44-46).

elsewhere.note: I may impart some spiritual gift.
You who are spiritual, restore him.
Every spiritual blessing in Christ.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Belonging to the ordinary human life (psychē, "soul"), without the Spirit. "The natural person" does not accept the things of God's Spirit (2:14). The same word describes the present body in 15:44, and means "a body suited to this age," not an evil one.

elsewhere.note: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.
This wisdom is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
Natural, devoid of the Spirit.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To examine closely, as in a legal inquiry. Paul says the spiritual person "examines" all things (2:14-15) and that he himself is "examined" by the Lord (4:3-4). The word describes careful, serious evaluation, not casual criticism.

elsewhere.note: They searched the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
My defense to those who examine me.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Of the flesh, meaning living by ordinary human, self-centered ways rather than the Spirit. Paul says the Corinthians are still "fleshly" because of jealousy and strife (3:1-4).

elsewhere.note: If the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they owe it to serve them in material things.
If we have sown spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap material things?
Not in fleshly wisdom.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A baby or very young child, one who cannot yet speak or reason as an adult. Paul uses it for believers who are immature (3:1) and in his poem on love for the childish way of speaking and thinking he has left behind (13:11).

elsewhere.note: You have revealed them to infants.
No longer children, tossed to and fro.
Everyone who partakes of milk is an infant.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A co-worker, someone who works alongside others. Paul uses it for himself and Apollos as "God's fellow workers" (3:9), and elsewhere for friends like Timothy, Priscilla, and Aquila.

elsewhere.note: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers.
Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow worker.
Titus is my partner and fellow worker.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The foundation of a building. Paul says Jesus Christ is the only foundation (3:10-12), and in Ephesians the apostles and prophets are described as a foundation with Christ as the cornerstone.

elsewhere.note: Built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets.
The city which has the foundations.
He laid the foundation on the rock.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The inner sanctuary of a temple, where the god dwelt, as distinct from the whole temple area (hieron). Paul says the church is "the temple of God" (3:16-17), and later that the body is "the temple of the Holy Spirit" (6:19).

range.note: The inner house of a god.

elsewhere.note: You are the temple of the living God.
A holy temple in the Lord.
I saw no temple in it.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To test something to see whether it is genuine, as metal is tested by fire, and so to approve what passes. Paul uses it for the fire that tests each person's work (3:13) and later for examining oneself before the Lord's Supper (11:28).

elsewhere.note: So that you may prove what is the will of God.
Test all things; hold fast to what is good.
The testing of your faith, more precious than gold.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The church is "God's building" (3:9); in other chapters the word means "building up" (8:1; 14:3-26).

elsewhere.note: Pursue the things that build up one another.
The whole building, fitted together.

notes: A household manager, often a trusted slave, who looked after the master's property and affairs. Paul calls himself and Apollos "stewards of God's mysteries," who must be found faithful (4:1-2).

range.note: Keeper of funds, as with Erastus.

elsewhere.note: Who then is the faithful and wise steward?
An overseer must be blameless, as God's steward.
Good stewards of God's varied grace.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Paul speaks of "God's wisdom in a mystery" (2:7) and calls himself a steward of God's mysteries (4:1).

range.note: Something hidden until it is disclosed.
In wider Greek, the secret rites of a cult.

elsewhere.note: The revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages.
The mystery was made known to me by revelation.

notes: "God revealed them to us through the Spirit" (2:10).

elsewhere.note: The righteousness of God is revealed.
You revealed them to infants.

notes: "We have Christ's mind" (2:16).

elsewhere.note: Be transformed by the renewing of your mind.
He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.

notes: To inflate, like a bag filled with air. Paul uses it for pride in this letter more than anywhere else (4:6, 4:18-19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4), and sets it against love, which "is not puffed up."

elsewhere.note: Puffed up without cause by his fleshly mind.

notes: What is wiped off, scraped away, or washed off, so refuse or scum. In 4:13 Paul says the apostles are treated as "the filth of the world." It could also describe a person offered as a sacrifice to save others.

elsewhere.note: The apostles are treated as the dirt wiped off by all.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "The Kingdom of God is not in word, but in power" (4:20); later Paul warns that wrongdoers will not inherit it (6:9-10).

range.note: The right and power to rule.
The people or territory a king rules.
The age when God's will is done on earth as in heaven.

elsewhere.note: The Kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace.
The Kingdom of God is at hand.

notes: Yeast or sourdough starter, a bit of old dough that makes new dough rise. Because a small amount spreads through the whole lump, it became a picture for something small that spreads, usually evil in the New Testament. At Passover, Jews removed all leaven from their homes (Exodus 12). Paul uses the picture in 5:6-8 and Galatians 5:9.

elsewhere.note: Beware of the yeast of the Pharisees.
The kingdom is like yeast a woman hid in flour.
A little yeast leavens the whole lump.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To clean out thoroughly. Paul says "clean out the old yeast" (5:7) as Jewish households searched their homes to remove leaven before Passover.

elsewhere.note: If anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed" (5:7).

elsewhere.note: The day of Unleavened Bread came, when the Passover lamb must be sacrificed.
The disciples ask where to prepare the Passover.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Paul begins with a case of porneia "not even among the Gentiles" (5:1), and tells them to "flee porneia" (6:18).
uncertain: Exactly what porneia covers in Jesus' exception (adultery, an unlawful marriage, or sexual sin more broadly) is debated, as is how the clause relates to Mark and Luke, which don't have it.

range.note: The earliest sense, from the word for a prostitute.
As in Leviticus 18, which Acts 15 echoes.

elsewhere.note: From the heart come sexual immorality.
Abstain from sexual immorality.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "Deliver such a one to Satan" (5:5).

range.note: Pass something on, as a teaching.

elsewhere.note: God gave them up to uncleanness.
Whom I delivered to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "You would have to leave the world" (5:10); "the saints will judge the world" (6:2).

elsewhere.note: God so loved the world.
He was in the world, and the world was made through him.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: "The destruction of the flesh" (5:5).

elsewhere.note: Those who live according to the flesh.
The flesh lusts against the Spirit.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To inherit, to receive as an heir. Used in the Old Testament for inheriting the land, and in the New Testament for inheriting the Kingdom or eternal life. Paul says the unrighteous "will not inherit the Kingdom of God" (6:9-10).

elsewhere.note: The meek will inherit the earth.
Inherit the kingdom prepared for you.
Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

notes: Soft, as in soft clothing (Matthew 11:8). In 6:9 it is one of the words in the list of wrongdoers, where its meaning is debated: commentators have taken it to mean morally weak, effeminate, or a passive partner in a same-sex relationship. Read this verse alongside commentaries on the word.

elsewhere.note: A man dressed in soft clothing.
A man dressed in soft clothing.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

gloss: one who lies with a male (debated)
notes: A rare word that appears first in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10. It is made of two words, "male" and "bed." Its precise meaning is debated: some take it to refer to male same-sex intercourse, perhaps echoing Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 in Greek, and others to some form of exploitation. Look at the discussion in commentaries.

elsewhere.note: Also in a list of wrongdoers.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: To buy in the marketplace (agora). Paul uses it for being "bought with a price" (6:20; 7:23), a picture of redemption that would be easily understood in a city with a slave market.

elsewhere.note: Send them away to buy themselves something to eat.
Denying the Master who bought them.
You purchased people for God with your blood.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The body, a person as a physical being. In this letter it is a major word (47 times): Paul argues that the body belongs to the Lord (6:13-20), that the church is Christ's body (12), and that the body will be raised (15). It is not just a shell but the person.

elsewhere.note: Present your bodies a living sacrifice.
This is my body.
The building up of the body of Christ.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A limb or part of the body. Paul says the Corinthians' bodies are "members of Christ" (6:15), and in chapter 12 each believer is a member of one body.

elsewhere.note: As in one body we have many members.
The tongue is a small member.
We are members of one another.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A gift freely given (from charis, "grace"). In 1 Corinthians it names the abilities God gives for the good of the church (1:7; 7:7; 12:4-31), and Paul stresses that the gifts are given, not earned.

elsewhere.note: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us.
The free gift of God is eternal life.
Don't neglect the gift that is in you.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A concession, allowance, or pardon. In 7:6 Paul says that what he has just said about marital relations is a concession, not a command.

elsewhere.note: This I say by way of concession.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Not married (a- "not" plus gamos "marriage"). Paul uses it for single people, probably including widowers and divorced persons, in his advice about marriage and singleness (7:8, 7:11, 7:32-34).

elsewhere.note: The unmarried woman is concerned about the Lord's things.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: A young unmarried woman, usually understood to be a virgin. Chapter 7:25-38 is Paul's advice on "virgins," and scholars debate whether he means daughters under a father's care, or engaged couples, or unmarried people in general; the Greek of 7:36-38 is unclear.

range.note: A woman who has not had sexual relations.

elsewhere.note: The virgin will be with child.
A virgin pledged to be married.
Ten virgins took their lamps.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: One without faith (a- "not" plus pistis "faith"), an unbeliever, a person outside the faith. The word appears often in this letter for neighbors and spouses (6:6; 7:12-15; 10:27; 14:22-24).

elsewhere.note: Do not be unbelieving, but believing.
Don't be unequally yoked with unbelievers.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Free, not a slave. Paul says a slave who has been called in the Lord is the Lord's "free person," and that those who were free are Christ's slaves (7:21-22).

elsewhere.note: There is neither slave nor free.
The Jerusalem above is free.
Free and slave, small and great.

notes: Necessity, compulsion, or pressure. In 7:26 it appears with "present" to describe the "present distress," and in 7:37 it describes a man who is not under any compulsion. The exact crisis Paul means is unknown.

elsewhere.note: Great distress on the land.
In great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships.
Not by compulsion but of your own accord.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: The outward form or appearance of something. Paul says the "form of this world" is passing away (7:31), perhaps as a stage set is taken down at the end of a play. The English word "scheme" comes from it.

elsewhere.note: The form of this world is passing away.

review.note: Hand-written first draft from general knowledge. Check against commentaries and a lexicon.

notes: Knowledge, from the verb ginōskō, "to know." In this letter it is something the Corinthians prize and sometimes boast about (1:5; 8:1-11; 12:8; 13:2, 13:8). Paul says knowledge by itself puffs up, but love builds up.

elsewhere.note: The depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God.
The light of the knowledge of God's glory.
All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

notes: A compound word, "idol-sacrifice," meaning meat that had been offered in a pagan temple. In Corinth, such meat was served in temple dining rooms, sold in the market, and served at private dinners. Chapters 8 through 10 deal with it.

elsewhere.note: Abstain from things sacrificed to idols.
To eat things sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality.

notes: An image of a god. Paul agrees with the Corinthians that "an idol is nothing in the world" (8:4), meaning there is no real god behind it, but in chapter 10 warns that demons are active behind pagan worship.

elsewhere.note: They offered a sacrifice to the idol.
You turned to God from idols.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

gloss: to be weak, to be sick
notes: To be weak or ill. In chapter 8 it describes the conscience of those who are not confident that eating idol food is harmless (8:7-12).

elsewhere.note: Accept him who is weak in faith.
When I am weak, then am I strong.
The sick were healed.
